## Foundations of Differential Privacy Against Timing Attacks

## Abstract

The framework of differential privacy (DP), introduced by Dwork, McSherry, Nissim, and Smith in 2006, provides rigorous mathematical guarantees on what an algorithm’s output can reveal about its input. However, real systems often expose information through observable channels beyond the algorithm’s output. In particular, the algorithm’s runtime may also be observable, creating a timing side channel through which information about the input can leak. This thesis studies differential privacy in the presence of timing side channels. We begin by developing a theoretical framework for reasoning about timing-private DP programs, whose privacy must hold under the joint observation of their output and execution time. We then show that if a DP program has bounded timing stability, meaning that small changes to the input induce only limited changes in runtime, one can add carefully calibrated randomized delay to achieve (ε, δ)- joint output/timing privacy (JOT-DP). This framework supports modular reasoning about the runtime behavior of programs and yields efficient constructions of timing-private DP programs for common data analysis tasks. Building on this framework, the thesis makes three further contributions.

1. We show that timing side channels are a practical threat to real implementations of differential privacy. In particular, we identify timing vulnerabilities in popular DP libraries across a range of common DP data analysis tasks, and we develop an auditing methodology for quantifying the resulting privacy loss when both outputs and runtimes are observable.

2. We study pure timing privacy (δ = 0) in the unbounded setting, where dataset size itself is sensitive and can be arbitrarily large. We give efficient constructions of pure JOT-DP programs in this setting, show that the achievable error depends on the model of computation, and prove matching lower bounds for the computational models we study, showing that these constructions are optimal.

3. We extend the study of timing privacy to the user-level setting, where privacy is defined with respect to adding or removing all records contributed by a single user. We show that bounded per-user contributions allow ordinary user-level DP algorithms to be transformed into JOT-DP programs with only small statistical error in their output distributions. In contrast, when user contributions are unbounded, even approximate (δ > 0) timing-private guarantees are incompatible with nontrivial utility. We then recover positive results under natural structural assumptions on the input.

## Chapter 1

## Introduction

### 1.1 Private Data Analysis and Timing Side Channels

Much of the modern world relies on the collection and analysis of data about individuals. Such data

enable scientific discovery and power a wide range of modern technologies, from search engines and

digital advertising to large-scale machine learning models. However, collecting and using such data can

pose significant privacy risks to the individuals from whom the data is collected [Swe00, DN03, NS06,

DY08, Abo18]. A natural goal is therefore to enable useful analysis of datasets about individuals while

limiting what can be learned about any one individual from the result of the analysis.

Differential privacy (DP), introduced by Dwork, McSherry, Nissim, and Smith [DMNS06],

formalizes this goal by requiring that the output distribution of an algorithm be nearly the same on any

pair of neighboring datasets, meaning datasets that differ in one individual’s data. Formally,

Definition 1.1.1 (Differential Privacy [DMNS06]). Let M : X →Y be a randomized algorithm. We

say M is (ε, δ)-differentially private if for every pair of neighboring datasets x, x′ ∈X and every subset

S ⊆Y,

Pr[M(x) ∈S] ≤eε · Pr[M(x′) ∈S] + δ.

We say that M satisfies pure differential privacy (and call it ε-differentially private) when δ = 0 and

approximate differential privacy when δ > 0.

Intuitively, differential privacy bounds how much the output can change one’s ability to infer

whether any particular individual’s data was included in the input. The parameters ε and δ control the

strength of this guarantee, with smaller values corresponding to stronger privacy. In typical applica-

tions, ε is taken to be a small constant and δ is taken to be cryptographically small (in particular, negli-

gible in the dataset size n). One common way DP algorithms achieve privacy is by adding carefully cali-

brated random noise to the result of a computation. This creates a privacy-utility tradeoff, since adding

more noise provides stronger privacy but also makes the released output less accurate and therefore less

useful.

However, this definition only constrains what is revealed by the algorithm’s output. In real sys-

tems, one may observe other aspects of the computation as well, including the program’s runtime. If

the runtime is correlated with the input or with internal randomness that is intended to remain hidden,

then observing the runtime may reveal information that is not protected by the standard definition of

differential privacy. Such leakage is known as a timing side channel. This exposes a gap between the ide-

alized guarantees of differential privacy and the behavior of real implementations.

As a motivating example, consider the textbook differentially private algorithm known as ran-

domized response [War65], shown in Figure 1.1. This algorithm is often motivated by surveys involving

sensitive questions that respondents may be afraid to answer truthfully if their answers were revealed

directly. In its simplest form, the algorithm takes as input a bit x ∈{0, 1} encoding the respondent’s

true answer and proceeds as follows. It first flips a fair coin. If the coin comes up heads, it outputs the

true bit x. If the coin comes up tails, it flips a second fair coin and outputs the outcome of that coin

flip instead. In this way, the released answer is sometimes the respondent’s true answer and sometimes

an independent random bit, giving the respondent plausible deniability. At the same time, because the

output remains correlated with the input, a surveyor who collects many such randomized responses can

still use them to accurately estimate the fraction of the population for which x = 1. Importantly, one

can show that this algorithm satisfies ε-differential privacy for ε = ln(3).

However, the implementation of randomized response given in Figure 1.1 contains a severe tim-

ing side channel. Suppose we use the number of instructions executed by the program as a proxy for

runtime. Then the runtime reveals which branch of the algorithm was taken. An execution that halts

after 4 instructions must have returned at line 4, in which case the output equals the true input bit x.

An execution that runs for 6 instructions must instead have continued to lines 6 and 7, in which case

the joint observation of output and runtime is blatantly non-private.

The randomized response example illustrates the central lesson of the thesis. An implementa-

tion can satisfy differential privacy with respect to its output distribution and still leak sensitive infor-

mation through its runtime. In practice, such leakage can arise through data-dependent control flow,

variable-time subroutines whose running time depends on hidden intermediate values or internal ran-

domness, or microarchitectural effects such as cache behavior and branch prediction. This leads to the

central question of the thesis: how can we reason about and secure differentially private implementa-

tions in the presence of timing side channels?

### 1.2 Motivation for this Study

Timing side channels are a long-standing concern in computer security. In a timing attack, an adver-

sary uses variation in a program’s execution time to infer information about secrets that are not ex-

plicitly released. Such attacks have been used to break or weaken cryptographic implementations and

protocols, including Diffie-Hellman, RSA, and DSS implementations [Koc96], TLS implementa-

tions [BT11, AFP13], AES implementations [Ber05, OST06], and systems affected by speculative exe-

cution [KHF+20, LSG+18]. These attacks show that protecting the abstract input-output behavior of

a system is not always enough when the implementation exposes execution-dependent signals.

Differential privacy faces an analogous implementation problem. The formal guarantee of DP

is usually stated for the output of a randomized computation, but real implementations also expose

execution behavior such as runtime. Prior work had already shown that this kind of timing leakage can

invalidate the guarantees of DP mechanisms. For example, Haeberlen, Pierce, and Narayan [HPN11]

demonstrated such a vulnerability by attacking the PINQ system [McS09], an interactive framework

in which an analyst can submit queries to a sensitive dataset and receive a differentially private result.

PINQ allows analysts to write user-defined programs that are intended to satisfy differential privacy

with respect to their outputs. However, this output guarantee does not prevent a query’s runtime from

depending on sensitive properties of the input. Figure 1.2 gives a representative example of the kind

of user-defined query considered by Haeberlen et al. The query always returns the constant 0, but by

sleeping only when it encounters a record belonging to Bob, its runtime reveals whether Bob is present

in the dataset.

4


<!-- Page 14 -->


Subsequent work showed that timing side channels are not limited to user-defined queries. Jin,

McMurtry, Rubinstein, and Ohrimenko [JMRO21] demonstrated that the discrete noise samplers used

by many DP algorithms can themselves leak information through their runtime. In particular, they

showed that the runtime of these samplers can be correlated with the magnitude of the sampled noise

used to privatize the mechanism’s output. As a result, an attacker who can infer the sampled noise from

the runtime can strip that noise away from the output and thereby recover the underlying sensitive

value.

These works established that timing leakage is a real concern for differentially private imple-

mentations, but they focused primarily on user-defined queries and sampling algorithms. The broader

scope of timing side channels in differential privacy systems remained poorly understood. In particular,

it was unclear how widespread such vulnerabilities are in real DP libraries, how much privacy loss they

can cause in practice, and how to reason about them at the level of general program design rather than

individual examples.

More broadly, this thesis fits into a well-established line of work showing that there can be se-

rious mismatches between the idealized guarantees of differential privacy and the behavior of real im-

plementations. Timing side channels are one instance of this more general phenomenon. Other exam-

ples include vulnerabilities caused by finite-precision arithmetic, where privacy analyses often assume

idealized real arithmetic but implementations instead use floating-point numbers [Mir12, JMRO21],

and implementation errors that arise when the sensitivity of a computation is analyzed under idealized

arithmetic but the deployed system instead uses saturating or otherwise bounded arithmetic [CSVW22].

These kinds of discrepancies have already motivated new lines of research on differential privacy on fi-

nite models of computation [BV18]. The broader lesson is that proving differential privacy for an ab-

stract mathematical mechanism is not always enough to guarantee privacy for its implementation. One

must also account for the computational model and the side channels available to the adversary.

Timing side channels are only one part of the broader problem of defending differentially

private implementations. Under stronger threat models, an adversary may be able to observe other

aspects of a program’s execution as well, such as memory access patterns [GO96] (e.g., cache behav-

ior [Ber05, OST06]), network activity [Ray01], or power consumption [KJJ99]. Protecting against

such side channels may require different privacy notions and different implementation techniques.

Thus, timing privacy should be understood as one part of the broader effort to align the guarantees of

differential privacy with the behavior of real systems.

### 1.3 Overview of Our Contributions

This thesis studies differential privacy in the presence of timing side channels. It develops a framework

for reasoning about timing-private programs, shows that timing attacks arise in real systems, and stud-

ies when such guarantees can and cannot be achieved in several important settings.

The organization of the thesis and its main contributions are as follows.

• Preliminaries. In Chapter 2, we introduce the definitions and notation used throughout the

thesis. In particular, we define the computational models in which we study timing side chan-

nels, formalize dataset spaces and adjacency notions, and review the differential privacy defini-

tions and basic tools that underlie the later chapters.

• A framework for differential privacy against timing attacks. In Chapter 3, we develop a

general framework for reasoning about differentially private programs when both their output

and runtime are observable. Within this framework, we define new privacy notions that account

for timing side-channel leakage and develop tools for proving that programs satisfy these guar-

antees. We characterize timing-stable programs, whose runtimes can change by only a bounded

amount on neighboring inputs, and show that adding carefully calibrated randomized delay to

them yields timing-private programs. The framework also supports modular reasoning through

chaining and composition. We implement these ideas in a proof-of-concept extension of the

OpenDP Library [SVM+a].

• Timing attacks on real-world implementations of differential privacy. In Chapter 4,

we conduct an empirical study showing that timing side channels are not merely a theoreti-

cal concern. We demonstrate that popular open-source differential privacy libraries, including

OpenDP [SVM+a], PyDP [Ope23a], and diffprivlib [HBMAL19], contain timing side-channel

vulnerabilities across a range of commonly used transformations and measurements. These vul-

nerabilities arise not only in user-defined functions and sampling routines, which were already

known to contain timing side channels [HPN11, JMRO21], but also in seemingly innocuous op-

erations such as sorting, filtering, and floating-point multiplication. We also develop an auditing

methodology for estimating lower bounds on privacy loss when both outputs and runtimes are

observable, allowing us to quantify the severity of these attacks in practice.

• Securing differential privacy in the unbounded setting. In Chapter 5, we study whether

pure timing privacy (δ = 0) is achievable in the unbounded setting, where dataset size itself is

sensitive and can be arbitrarily large. This question is important because many standard algo-

rithms satisfy pure DP, and it is therefore desirable to preserve pure DP in their implementations

as well. By contrast, the general constructions from Chapter 3 achieve timing privacy by adding

randomized delay to timing-stable programs, and this approach inherently yields only approxi-

mate timing privacy. To this end, we give the first efficient constructions of pure timing-private

DP algorithms in the unbounded setting. In the RAM model, we transform upper-bounded

pure timing-private programs into unbounded ones while preserving the original output distri-

bution up to small total variation distance, with error probability that can decay polynomially

in the dataset size. In weaker models, we show that a constant error probability is unavoidable.

We also prove matching lower bounds showing that these guarantees are essentially optimal. As

corollaries, we obtain pure timing-private analogues of standard unbounded-DP mechanisms

whose accuracy closely matches that of their non-timing-private counterparts.

• Extending timing privacy to the user-level DP setting. The final contribution of the the-

sis, in Chapter 6, initiates the study of timing privacy under user-level adjacency, where privacy

is defined with respect to adding or removing all records contributed by a single user. The main

difficulty is that, unlike in the record-level setting considered in Chapters 3 and 5, a single user

that when per-user contributions are bounded, ordinary user-level DP programs can be com-

Taken together, these contributions develop the foundations for differential privacy in the pres-

## Chapter 2

## Preliminaries

This chapter introduces the definitions and notation used throughout the thesis. We begin by defin-

ing the computational model and execution environments. We then define datasets and the distance

metrics used to capture adjacency.

### 2.1 Models of Computation

A program’s runtime is determined by its computational model. In the idealized RAM model, runtime

is typically measured by the number of instructions executed before halting. On physical systems, how-

ever, runtime may depend on many additional factors. For example, for a C program running on an

x86 processor, runtime might be measured in CPU cycles, but the same program on the same hardware

can still exhibit different runtimes because of factors such as microcode patches [Sta03]. Runtime can

also vary because of nondeterministic effects such as cache interference from concurrent executions.

Accordingly, we allow both a program’s output and runtime to depend on an execution en-

vironment env ∈E. Formally, an execution environment is any state in the computational model

that can affect program execution, such as the contents of uninitialized memory, the initial values of

CPU registers, or other relevant machine state. We treat the program’s input as part of the execution

environment, and we write supp(P(x, env)) = ∅whenever the input x and environment env are

incompatible.

Definition 2.1.1 (Input/Environment Compatibility). Our computational models come with an in-

put/environment compatibility relation, and when an environment env ∈E is incompatible with an

9


<!-- Page 19 -->


input x ∈X for program P, we define supp(P(x, env)) = ∅.

Whether a pair (x, env) is compatible depends on the computational model. For example, un-

der the calling convention for C functions on modern x86 hardware, the EBP and ESP registers specify

the base and top of the stack frame in memory. If these registers point to conflicting memory locations,

or if the stack does not contain the correct setup for the function’s input arguments, then the execu-

tion environment is incompatible with the function’s input. We give further examples of incompatible

input/environment pairs when discussing the RAM model.

Definition 2.1.2 (Program Execution). A randomized program P : X × E →Y × E takes in an

input x ∈X, and an execution environment env ∈E, and outputs a value y ∈Y denoted by the

random variable out(P(x, env)). The execution of P may also induce changes on the environment,

and we indicate the new state of the environment as the random variable outenv(P(x, env)).

Definition 2.1.3 (Program Runtime). Suppose that our computational model’s runtime is measured

in units T ⊆R≥0 (e.g., T = N if runtime measures the number of executed instructions). Then we

denote the runtime of program P : X × E →Y × E within execution environment env on input x to

be the random variable TP(x, env) ∈T .

We can drop the environment env from our notation when a program’s output and runtime

is independent of the environment. We call such programs pure to follow standard programming lan-

guages terminology, but not to be confused with pure DP.

Definition 2.1.4 (Output-Pure Programs). A program P : X × E →Y × E is output-pure if there

exists a (possibly randomized) function f : X →Y such that for all x ∈X and all input-compatible

env ∈E, f(x) is identically distributed to out(P(x, env)).

Definition 2.1.5 (Timing-Pure Programs). A program P : X × E →Y × E is timing-pure if there

exists a (possibly randomized) function f : X →T such that for all x ∈X, and all input-compatible

env ∈E, f(x) is identically distributed to TP(x, env).

We remark that the standard definition of differential privacy implicitly assumes that programs

are output-pure, and in fact, its composition and post-processing theorems fail if that is not the case.

RAM Model. Throughout this thesis, we use the idealized RAM and Word RAM models of com-

putation to give proof-of-concept results for our framework. The RAM model consists of an infinite

sequence of memory cells, each of which can hold an arbitrarily large natural number. Variables are

stored in registers, and the model supports basic arithmetic, logical, and memory operations. Programs

also include conditional jump instructions (if CONDITIONAL goto LINE), which allow us to sim-

ulate the usual if, else, and while constructs.1 Many of our RAM programs are randomized and use

a RAND(n) instruction to sample a uniform random integer in {0, . . . , n}. We define the runtime of

a RAM program to be the number of basic instructions executed before halting, where halting is in-

dicated by a HALT command. Thus the space of runtime values is T = N. The model also includes

built-in variables input_len and input_ptr, which indicate the length |x| of the input x and the

memory location at which the input begins. Similarly, every program writes its output to a memory

location indexed by output_ptr and sets output_len to indicate the length of the output.

RAM programs do not assume anything about memory locations outside the region con-

taining the input, and must initialize any such memory before using it. This matches the behavior

of languages such as C, where memory returned by malloc2 is not assumed to be initialized to zero.

As a result, our RAM model includes a limited form of nondeterminism, since a program may read

values from uninitialized memory. The space of execution environments E therefore consists of all

possible memory configurations together with the initial values of the built-in variables input_ptr,

input_len, output_ptr, and output_len.

Definition 2.1.6 (RAM Environment). The environment env of a RAM program is the infinite se-

quence (v0, v1, . . . , ) such that M[i] = vi for all i along with the values stored by the built-in variables

input_ptr, input_len, output_ptr, and output_len.

Remark. A program’s environment includes the program’s input x by definition, and similarly, a pro-

gram’s output environment outenv(P(x, env)) includes the program’s output out(P(x, env)).

Not every environment is compatible with every input. For example, an environment in which

all memory locations are uninitialized is incompatible with any nonempty input. More generally, if

(x, env) is compatible, then the memory locations specified by input_ptr and input_len in env

must contain the input x. Finally, most of our RAM programs are pure and do not interact with unini-

tialized memory. For such programs, both the output and runtime are independent of the execution

environment for all compatible pairs (x, env).

## Chapter 3

## A Framework for Differential Privacy

## Against Timing Attacks

This chapter develops a framework for reasoning about differential privacy in the presence of timing

side channels. Our goal is to understand what privacy should mean when an adversary can observe not

only a program’s output, but also its execution time, and to develop general tools for constructing pro-

grams that satisfy such guarantees.

A natural first response to timing leakage is to enforce constant-time execution. This approach

is standard in cryptography, where implementations are often designed so that secret inputs do not

affect observable timing behavior [BCS13, CSB+17]. For differentially private data analysis, however,

constant-time execution is often too blunt an instrument. It may require the program to assume or re-

veal a public upper bound on the input size, to give up the ability to process arbitrarily large datasets,

and to incur substantial overhead by padding every execution to the worst-case runtime. More impor-

tantly, it is stronger than what differential privacy typically requires, since differential privacy allows for

non-negligible information leakage (unlike encryption).

This motivates a more flexible approach. Rather than requiring a program to take exactly the

same amount of time on every input, one can ask whether its runtime can itself be made private. One

possible way to do this is to add random delay before releasing the output, much as random noise is

added to privatize a program’s output. This approach was first suggested by Haeberlen, Pierce, and

Narayan [HPN11], and while compelling, it leaves two basic questions unanswered.

1. What does it mean for a program’s runtime to be differentially private?

### 3.5 Chaining and Composition

Software libraries such as OpenDP and Tumult Core [GHV20, BBD+22, SVM+b] support chaining

together multiple algorithms in a modular fashion to create more complex mechanisms with provable

stability and privacy guarantees. Motivated by these libraries, we extend our framework to support sim-

ilar functionality. Specifically, we discuss properties of timing-stable programs that are combined to

create more complex functionality such as chaining and composition.

## Chaining Timing-Stable Programs

While timing stability bounds the differences in program execution time for a single program P, we are

often interested in chaining together multiple programs, e.g., executing program P2 on the output of

program P1. For such chaining operations, we use the notation (P2 ◦P1)(x, env1) interchangeably

with P2(P1(x, env1), env2) for some execution environment env2 (see below).

Definition 3.5.1 (Chaining-compatible Programs). We say that programs P1 : X × E →Y × E and

P2 : Y × E →Z × E are chaining-compatible if there exists a program (P2 ◦P1) and a constant c such

that for inputs x ∈X and environments env1 ∈E, there exists a (possibly random) env2 ∈E such

that we have:

out((P2 ◦P1)(x, env1)) = out(P2(out(P1(x, env1)), env2))

and

T(P2◦P1)(x, env1) = TP1(x, env1) + TP2(out(P1(x, env1)), env2) + c.

Here we allow the random variable env2 to be arbitrarily correlated with x, as well as the output and

runtime of P1(x, env1), but should be independent of the coin tosses of P2.

Remark. If the construction of P2 ◦P1 in the computational model does not modify the environ-

ment when chaining programs together, then env2 equals outenv(P1(x, env1)). However, real-world

systems often modify the environment before executing sequential programs, e.g., setting up CPU reg-

isters.

## Attacking Partition Selection

In many private data analysis tasks, it is necessary to determine which groups or partitions in a dataset

should be included in a release. This decision can itself be sensitive. For example, suppose a medical

researcher at a university conducts a survey of students with a particular health condition and releases

aggregate statistics grouped by nationality. If the output includes a group for a particular nationality,

## Pure Timing Privacy in the Unbounded

## Setting

Chapter 3 developed a general technique for constructing timing-private programs. The basic approach

was to bound a program’s timing stability, and then add randomized delay scaled according to that

bound to the program’s execution. However, this approach has two important limitations. First, it in-

herently yields only approximate JOT-DP, even when the original program is pure DP in its output.

Second, it applies only to programs that are timing-stable, and therefore does not apply to computa-

tions with superlinear runtime (Lemma 3.2.11).

These limitations are not prohibitive in the bounded DP setting. When a public bound on

input size is available, one can often obtain pure JOT-DP simply by padding execution to the worst-case

runtime over all inputs within that bound. In the unbounded setting, however, the dataset size itself is

sensitive and may grow arbitrarily large, so this kind of worst-case padding is no longer available.

This chapter studies whether one can nevertheless obtain pure JOT-DP in the unbounded set-

ting while preserving the utility and efficiency of standard DP algorithms as much as possible. A natu-

ral starting point is a result of Ben Dov, David, Naor, and Tzalik [BDDNT23], who showed that pure

DP programs in the unbounded setting can be converted into pure JOT-DP programs. Their result es-

tablished that pure timing privacy is possible in principle, but it left several basic questions unresolved.

In particular, their transformation incurs a constant additive increase in error probability, is computa-

tionally inefficient, and is analyzed in a more restricted model in which runtime is measured only by the

number of random bits used. This leaves open whether, in more standard computational models, one

can obtain pure JOT-DP with asymptotically vanishing error and with implementations that remain

efficient.

In this chapter, we address these questions. We show that the achievable utility of pure JOT-

DP in the unbounded setting depends in an essential way on the computational model. In a random-

ized RAM model where the dataset size is given, or can be computed in constant time, and random

numbers can be generated in constant time, one can achieve failure probability that vanishes polyno-

mially with the dataset size. By contrast, if the dataset size is not given, or if the model provides only

a random-bit generator, then an arbitrarily small constant failure probability is the best possible. We

complement these lower bounds with eﬃcient transformations that turn pure JOT-DP programs in the

upper-bounded setting into pure JOT-DP programs in the unbounded setting, while preserving the

original output distribution up to small total variation distance. As corollaries, we obtain pure timing-

private analogues of standard unbounded mechanisms whose accuracy closely matches that of their

non-timing-private counterparts.

## Chapter 6

## Timing Privacy for User-level DP Programs

In this chapter, we consider the user-level setting, where privacy is defined with respect to the addition

or removal of an entire user’s contribution rather than a single record. This setting is natural in appli-

cations where one user may generate many events, such as transactions, searches, clicks, telemetry, or

message metadata. We do not assume that the records contributed by one user appear contiguously in

memory. Instead, a user’s records may be scattered throughout the dataset, interleaved with the records

of many other users. In such settings, protecting only the presence or absence of a single record is often

too weak. The more appropriate goal is to protect whether an entire user’s contribution is present.

Extending the guarantees from Chapter 3 to this setting introduces new difficulties. In that

chapter, we achieved timing privacy by adding randomized delay to programs that are timing-stable,

meaning that their runtime changes by only a bounded amount on adjacent inputs. Under the notion

user-level adjacency (which we denote as dUserID, defined in Definition 2.2.6), however, many natural

user-level algorithms no longer fit this framework, even when each user contributes only a bounded

number of records. When a user’s records may be scattered throughout the input, even simple tasks

such as counting the number of distinct users require tracking which records belong to the same user

while scanning the dataset. Doing this in a timing-stable way is already nontrivial, so many basic user-

level computations fall outside the scope of the framework from Chapter 3.

The problem becomes harder still when there is no a priori bound on the number of records

contributed by a single user. In that regime, adding or removing one user can cause arbitrarily large

changes in runtime, even when the output sensitivity remains bounded. The natural question, then, is

when, and under what assumptions, timing privacy can still be achieved in the user-level setting.

We begin with two basic examples showing why achieving JOT-DP in the user-level setting is not straight-

forward using existing techniques.

Aggregating User Records. Consider a dataset x of transactions collected over time, where each

record contains a user identifier u and a value v ∈[0, b]. Because the records are ordered by time, a

total transaction value

or removing one user adds or removes all of that user’s transactions. If per-user contributions are un-

bounded, then q has unbounded global sensitivity with respect to dUserID. That is, adding or removing

a single user can change the value of q(x) by an arbitrarily large amount, since one user may contribute

arbitrarily many records.

In the setting where only output privacy is required, the standard remedy is to enforce a per-

user contribution cap. For example, one can truncate x so that each user u contributes at most B trans-

actions, say by keeping only the first B in time order, and then compute q on the truncated dataset.

After this preprocessing step, q has global sensitivity at most B · b with respect to dUserID, so it can be

released using standard DP mechanisms. This truncation may introduce bias when some users con-

However, this approach does not automatically yield JOT-DP. Enforcing a per-user cap re-

quires the algorithm to identify and count each user’s records across the dataset, which in general means

scanning the input and maintaining per-user state, such as counters. If one user contributes far more

than the cap, the algorithm must still process those records in order to identify and discard the excess.

As a result, the runtime can change by an unbounded amount between dUserID-neighboring datasets.

An observer who measures execution time may therefore detect the presence or absence of a heavy con-

tributor even when the output itself is differentially private.

### 6.3 Preprocessed Datasets

The impossibility result of Theorem 6.2.1 is partly driven by the input representation. Throughout this

paper, we model inputs as arbitrary sequences of user-labeled records. It is therefore natural to ask what

changes if the dataset is instead stored in a representation that is more aligned with user-level computa-

tion. In this section, we consider a different kind of relaxation, in which the dataset is first transformed

by a one-time preprocessing step that is not observable to the adversary.

A canonical preprocessing step is to group the records by user identifier, so that all records con-

tributed by the same user appear contiguously in memory. Once the input has this structure, tasks such

as counting users or truncating each user’s contribution become much more tractable from the per-

spective of timing privacy. The reason is that the computation no longer needs to recover a user’s con-

tribution from an arbitrary interleaving of records. Instead, each user’s contribution appears as a single

contiguous block, so once the program reaches the beginning of that block, it can process only the por-

tion it needs and then move directly to the next user.

A particularly convenient representation is one in which the first record of each user’s block

stores auxiliary metadata giving the size of that block.

Definition 6.3.1 (Grouped and length-annotated grouped representations). A dataset x ∈X is in

grouped form if all records contributed by the same user appear contiguously in memory.

## Chapter 7

## Conclusion

This thesis developed foundations for reasoning about differential privacy in the presence of timing

side channels. Standard definitions of differential privacy protect only the released output of an algo-

rithm, but real implementations may also reveal runtime. To account for this threat, we studied joint

output/timing privacy, treating mechanisms as programs in a computational model whose output

and runtime are both observable. We then developed stability notions for analyzing runtime leakage,

showed how randomized delay can transform timing-stable programs into timing-private programs,

and gave chaining and composition tools for reasoning about more complex computations.

We also showed that timing side channels arise in real implementations of differential privacy.

Through attacks on OpenDP, PyDP, and diffprivlib, we demonstrated that common operations such

as filtering, sorting, private partition selection, floating-point multiplication, and randomized response

can leak sensitive information through runtime. These attacks show that timing leakage is a practical

concern for deployed DP systems, not just a pathology of toy examples. They also motivate treating

runtime as part of the observable behavior of a DP implementation, rather than as an implementation

detail outside the privacy analysis.

Finally, we studied when timing privacy can and cannot be achieved. In the unbounded setting,

where dataset size is sensitive, we gave efficient constructions of pure JOT-DP programs and proved

lower bounds showing that the achievable error depends on the computational model. In the user-level

setting, we showed that bounded per-user contributions allow ordinary user-level DP programs to be

compiled into JOT-DP programs, while unbounded per-user contributions lead to strong impossibility

results. Taken together, these results show that timing behavior is a fundamental part of the privacy in-

terface of differentially private systems. They also show that, under appropriate structural assumptions,

DP implementations can be designed so that their observable behavior more faithfully matches their

formal privacy guarantees.
